summary: Cowlitz County site of a 30-foot pole tower and cabin (1935 or 1936); AWS post in 1942; destroyed in the 1962 Columbus Day Storm; footings reported in 2017.

facts.design: 30-foot pole tower with a 10-by-12 lookout house (1936 report); a 1942 AWS description gives a 40-foot tower with a small cab
facts.status_note: Register: destroyed in the Columbus Day Storm on October 12, 1962. WillhiteWeb's 2017 photo captions say all four footings remain in place.

staffing.status: Aircraft Warning Service post in 1942; named lookouts for 1952 to 1953 (FireLookout.com)

access.note: WillhiteWeb: roads go to within feet of the site, but a St. Helens Tree Farm Permit is needed to be legal. Brush and new trees are quickly overgrowing the site.

visit.trail_note: No tower stands. A tree farm permit is needed for a legal visit; the site is overgrown according to WillhiteWeb.

events.note: Register: 30-foot pole tower and cabin constructed in 1935. A 1936-labeled report entry, quoted by WillhiteWeb as a 1935 report, describes the same tower; a 1952 newspaper says built in 1936.

Aircraft Warning Service post. Activated March 16, 1942 under the Portland Filter Center. A 1942 AWS description gives a small cab on a 40-foot tower; caption names Harry Cobain as the 1942 lookout and AWS observers A.C. Lysons and R.W. Hukill.
Anna Wilkins profiled by the Longview Daily News on July 1, 1952; her job was spotting smokes over the Mount St. Helens Tree Farm
Warden planned to abandon the site within two years and erect a new tower about five miles north. No source says whether that tower was built.
Eva Ahlskog named as lookout for 1953
Register: abandoned in the 1940s (decade only). WillhiteWeb: reported abandoned in the later 1940s. The 1952 newspaper describes an active station, so the dates conflict.
Historic photos show the lookout still standing in 1960

Destroyed in the Columbus Day Storm on October 12, 1962 (register). A Longview Daily News item of the same date calls a mountain-top lookout the Wolf Creek Lookout and reports it blown over in the windstorm. The name differs from Wolf Point; linking the two is an inference from the storm date.
Second-growth forest on the site harvested sometime between 2001 and 2005; the third growth is near 20 feet tall now
Photo section captioned 'Remains in 2017' says all 4 footings remain in their original location

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register gives 1935. WillhiteWeb quotes the Washington Forest Fire Association 29th annual report as 1935, while a page labels the same report entry 1936. A 1952 Longview paper says it was built in 1936.

The register and the report describe a 30-foot tower. A 1942 AWS description gives 40 feet, and the 1952 Longview paper gives 50 feet and an altitude of 2,010 feet. The story uses the 30-foot construction height.
The register lists 2,996 feet (913 m). A 1952 Longview paper gives 2,010 feet, and the report quoted on the weebly page gives 3,100 feet.
The register says the 1940s. WillhiteWeb says reported abandoned in the later 1940s but standing in 1960. A 1952 Longview paper describes an active station with plans to abandon it within two years.

notes_for_editor: Status gone and the 1962 storm end are consistent across the register and the 1952 and 1962 Longview items. Height, built year, elevation and abandonment conflict across sources, and the story says so. Named staffing comes from one Longview Daily News profile and FireLookout.com, plus a WillhiteWeb caption. Footings rest on WillhiteWeb 2017 photo captions only. The 1962 newspaper calls the structure the Wolf Creek Lookout; the link to Wolf Point is an inference from the storm date, not stated in the source.
